The TPP is a massive "trade agreement" whose primary purpose seems to be regulating the internet. Unfortunately, we can't even begin to explain all the ways that it will affect you, because the actual text of the treaty has area 51 levels of security on it. Even member of Congress can only read it in a special room, alone, where they aren't allowed to take notes.

If it keeps with the trend of past free trade agreements, it's main function will be to change the laws in signatory countries in way that would not be able to be passed on their own do to it being political suicide. For example, when the US congress tried to pass SOPA, they met with huge resistance from the public and tech companies, and backed down. If they vote for the TPP, they're just ratify a trade treaty, if it just happens that the trade treaty in question contains provisions almost identical to that of SOPA (something that has been rumored to be true), that's not their fault.

How is a law allowed to be secret?

Edit: I'm serious, how is it justified?

Sorry your question is being ignored. I will try to answer.

These justifications of the TPP are "true" whether or not you think it is a good idea. There are costs to any actions, and maybe the costs of the TPP outweigh the benefits. So here are two benefits

First, there is a "production" justification. We can produce more when we break complex tasks into simpler tasks, and focus on making each of those simple tasks better. Because even simple tasks are actually pretty complicated when it comes to supply chains, you'll see different countries and different regions specializing in producing even simple things. National Public Radio had a n excellent series on how t-shirts are made. A lot goes into it, in a lot of countries.

So TPP reduces barriers to specialization in things like this. Maybe those barriers have other benefits. I dunno. But that's the production justification of the TPP. http://apps.npr.org/tshirt/#/title

Second, there's a security justification. CNN likes to focus on bombs or sanctions or summits, but real power is the ability to talk to someone. This is because almost every problem anyone actually faces is complicated, and there's a lot of "reasonable" takes on it. Take these little islands in the South China Sea. China can give you a really good reason why they are really China. Philippines can too. Vietnam can too. Everyone takes the issue seriously, and can tell you vital details that everyone else ignores or forgets about.

But everyone is super busy. Why should they make time on their schedule for your pet issue, your island or whatever, when there's lots of other issues with lots of other reasonable sides?

Well, you can also bring it up when you are talking about something else. The more you have to talk to, the more opportunities you have to bring anything up. And the TPP just coincidentally* [really, its a coincidence, really!] happens to involve a ton of countries that do a lot of business with China... but not China. So coincidentally* [really, its a coincidence, really!] we have a lot of opportunities to talk with a lot of countries that often do business with China... how convenient.

In the US the Congress is typically concerned with domestic policy, and currently the Republican Party (which is the more pro-business of the parties) is in charge of Congress. So Congress focuses more on the production justification, even if there are other sides that it is ignoring.

Likewise, the US President is more concerned with foreign policy, with the power that comes from talking to people, and so the President (who everyday faces an issue that would be easier if this-or-that person had a chance to talk to some other President or Prime Minister) is more concerned with the security justification.

Again, the TPP may or may not be a good idea. I've just shared two one-sided arguments. But they are fair arguments that are driving the pro side.

Hope this helps.

I also shared a link to a Planet Money episode on the secret NAFTA negotiations. In negotiations you never want the other side to know what you really want or don't want, but you want to know exactly what they want or don't want.

More broadly, in the US we don't have direct elections. To pass any kind of law or any kind of treaty, you cobble together the easiest coalition you can. 25 years ago we had a HUGE political debate around nafta, because labor unions were widely distributed and could organize a lot of people. So to counter a lot of noise, you need a lot of noise.

We don't have that now. The opposition to TPP is a lot of small groups. And because negotiations are secret it's dangerous for opponents to find any one cause to rally behind.

For instance, imagine everyone starts criticizing TPP for environmental reasons. But both the production justification and security justification don't really depend on environmental regulations much. So if everyone hates TPP for its environmental rules, they can just change those, while keeping everything else in place. This would break the anti-TPP coalition at a minimal cost to the pro side.

  1. Insurance Hikes: If that google engineer's warped thinking catches on, then we can eventually expect insurance companies to raise rates on people who can not afford or choose not to utilize a self driving car.   2. Personal Data: Sure, your phone is already leaking a ton of data about you. If you use a GPS everywhere, you're giving away even more... but you always have the option to just turn the phone off. When your car is driving you everywhere, advertisers know for certain that it's your car. Even if you drive it yourself, it's going to track your location. I've been uncomfortable about this sort of thing for a while. Someone posted an excellent link about this yesterday.

  3. Legal Ramifications: IANAL, but it seems to me there is a difference between my phone and my car directly reporting location/speed/heading. If it's my phone, I could still be in anyone's vehicle. If my car says I'm going too fast and my phone's location/speed/heading matches my car's, things are pretty iron clad. I worry about this kind of data becoming legally actionable. Live in a politically unstable country? The future just got even scarier. The thing about a self-driving car is that it can also be bricked. Remotely.

  4. Fees: Remember when no one knew what net neutrality was because no one even conceived of the alternative? Your car is now driven by a computer. All the analogies about paying to get out of the 'slow lane' could become literal.

  5. Spooks and Hackers: And you thought SWATting was dangerous. I'm sure it won't be as easy as SWATting, but you are 100% trusting that cybercriminals and agencies don't want you dead. Give in to our demands, or else... vroom vroom.

I'm sure there are other risks I'm not even thinking of. Look, I'm pretty damned far from being a luddite. I love technology and I think this tech has some amazing promise. But we've all seen what humanity has done with the internet and with smartphone technology. I'm not dead-set against self driving cars, but I am wary and not at all convinced the boons outweigh the risks in this case.

Of course, just like with smart phones, I expect that people won't be able to avoid them forever. 5 years ago, a smart phone was very useful. Today, it is all but required to function in society.

It's not about whether or not people find the format useful. It's about the matching algorithms Youtube uses and how commentary voiceover makes it harder for them to find matches. It's also about what kind of value the producer is adding to the video themselves. Explaining what the player is doing, reacting to things in the game as they unfold, and generally interacting with the viewer above and beyond simply presenting gameplay is one way a producer can say that they've contributed to the entertainment or educational value of what they're presenting.

In general, the guidelines for Youtubers producing gaming content are to provide commentary and/or royalty free music alongside the game audio, be careful of cutscenes, and don't use footage from game trailers. Someone who is just sitting down and recording gameplay and then doing simple edits or no edits at all and uploading to Youtube isn't really providing much of their own to the project which is why Youtube isn't in a rush to change their procedures and algorithms for the sake of "producers" presenting raw gameplay footage.

This is a real question. For many people prepping seems to be about kit. I think there are many outdoors enthusiasts who simply want to buy stuff for their hobby and need an excuse. This is fine, but it would be interesting to talk about how much it costs to deal with such and such a threat. only then can we do a cost benefit analysis on each threat.
How much should prepping cost? How long is string?

That's the tough thing about prepping. Ultimately, everyone has to decide what they really need in order to get by. For some, that will be a lot of expensive gear and weapons. For others, just adding some food storage, bottled water, and basic camping gear will have to be a good start. I, for one, own some weapons and a lot of camping gear already, so I'm looking for mostly food storage, water storage, and long term things like solar panels and seed for crops. The thing is, whatever the threat boils down to, do you have food, water, and shelter? Protection? When you really start looking around at what you already have, and what you need, it's much easier to figure out what it will cost to fill in the gaps.

This is good sense. I am coming to the view that one should spend about one percent of ones post tax income. This does not seem much but is actually a fair chunk of money for most people when added up.

I have to agree with you here. In my case most of my hobbies have overlapping gear which helps me justify it to myself. I enjoy fishing, hunting, rv'ing, backpacking, hiking, and shooting sports. Do I spend way to much money on these things? Probably.

Funny thing is, whenever I run into a new prepper the first thing I tell them is, "Don't make the same mistake I did. Odds are good the bottom isn't going to fall out tomorrow. Put together what you can from what you already have then start hitting the thrift stores and pawn shops."

I buy more things at pawn shops than anywhere else when it comes to gear. You can't beat the power of negotiation. Especially if you visit a place frequently enough that you can notice the things you want are still sitting there. Then it's simply a matter of informing them that whatever your looking at has been sitting on the shelf for 8 months and asking them if they'd be will to come down in price. The big brands won't but the smaller privately owned shops will normally.

It depends on your timeline among other variables. I find that the 50/30/20 budget is a good guideline and can also be applied to prepping. The idea is that 50% of your income should go toward fixed expenses or "needs," 20% should go toward investing for the future and 30% should be spent on fun or discretionary "wants."

So, save up 6 months worth of money to meet your fixed expenses- meaning what you need to spend to keep body and soul together, meet your legal obligations and maintain basic dignity. This could take different forms depending on what you're preparing for. You could save in your bank account, in bitcoin, in cash, in precious metals etc. Building up a 6 month supply of your regular food (that you'll use even if life continues on as normal) counts in this category. You'll need to eat even if the disaster is simply job loss, so this is an investment toward your security in any circumstance. Likewise having some savings that you can use to pay the bills is better than having to pay transaction costs and premiums trying to turn your precious metals into a mortgage payment.

Invest 10% of your income in some form of savings that will be of use if the system doesn't crash like a 401k IRA etc. (Paying down debt can also count here.) Then spend 10% of your income on non-consumable preps like equipment or a bug out location etc.

The "wants" or fun category is where you have the most discretion. Things like a cable bill or Netflix subscription fall here. Things like gardening, beer brewing or soap making are hobbies that can do double duty (if you genuinely enjoy doing them when life is normal.) I'd suggest that you don't spend more than 10% on "wants" that don't bring you enjoyment now.

In my mind, prepping is a way of life. It's not a hobby you can pack into a bag. It's a lifestyle that affects every decision you make. Where you live, how you live, etc. Don't get me wrong, bug out bags are fun and useful, but you need to have a destination in mind of where you're gonna bug out to, and make sure your bug out bag has everything to get you there.

Ideally, your bug out destination should have food, water, shelter, and whatever else you think you'll need, e.g., medicine, fuels, clothes, what have you. I'm a big fan of forest gardening. Perrenial crops will mostly maintain themselves once established. I've planted locally hardy fruit and but trees, bushes, and vines, as well as herbaceous perrenial medicines at my home where I intend to bugout. Plant them now, they won't have harvests for 5 years or so but then you'll have more than you'll ever need.

Rainwater catchment systems are in the works. Solar and wind energy collection systems will come eventually when I can afford them. Prepping is a way of life. When change is the only constant in the world, and your part of the world is on top, things can only deteriorate.
